content: The Black Death, also known as the Black Plague, is widely regarded as one of the most devastating pandemics in human history. It is traditionally attributed to the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which causes bubonic plague, though some recent theories suggest other diseases may have been involved. The pandemic is believed to have originated in Central Asia or India and spread to Europe in the 1340s. It is estimated to have caused the deaths of approximately 75 million people worldwide, with 25 to 50 million of those deaths occurring in Europe alone. The Black Death is thought to have killed between 30% and 60% of Europe’s population, reducing the global population from an estimated 450 million to between 350 and 375 million by the year 1400. Bubonic plague is believed to have recurred in Europe every generation with varying levels of virulence and mortality until the 1700s. Over 100 plague epidemics swept across Europe during this period. For example, the return of the plague in 1603 resulted in the deaths of 38,000 Londoners. Other notable outbreaks include the Italian Plague of 1629–1631, the Great Plague of Seville (1647–1652), the Great Plague of London (1665–1666), and the Great Plague of Vienna (1679). The term Black Death was first introduced in 1833. It is often thought to refer to the darkened skin of sufferers caused by subepidermal hemorrhages (purpura) and gangrene (acral necrosis). However, the term may also reflect the grim and dreadful nature of the pandemic. The Black Death was characterized by the appearance of buboes, which are swollen lymph nodes, often in the groin, neck, or armpits. These swellings oozed pus and bled. Most victims of the bubonic form of the plague died within four to seven days of infection. The disease also manifested in other forms, such as pneumonic plague, which attacked the lungs and had a mortality rate of 90–95%, and septicemic plague, which was almost universally fatal and caused symptoms such as high fever and purpura due to disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). The pandemic had profound social and economic consequences. It irreversibly altered Europe’s population and social structure, dealt a significant blow to the Roman Catholic Church, and led to widespread persecution of minorities, including Jews, foreigners, beggars, and lepers. The uncertainty of survival created a pervasive mood of morbidity, influencing cultural works such as Giovanni Boccaccio’s The Decameron. The origins of the Black Death remain a topic of debate. The most widely accepted theory is that it began in the steppes of Central Asia and spread along trade routes, such as the Silk Road, facilitated by Mongol armies and traders. It was reportedly introduced to Europe at the trading city of Caffa in the Crimea in 1347, where infected corpses were catapulted over city walls during a siege. Genoese traders fleeing Caffa brought the plague to Sicily, from where it spread throughout Europe. Pre-existing conditions such as war, famine, and climate changes exacerbated the severity of the pandemic. In China, the Mongol conquests disrupted agriculture and trade, leading to widespread famine and a population decline from 120 million to 60 million. In Europe, the end of the Medieval Warm Period brought harsher winters and reduced harvests, culminating in the Great Famine of 1315–1317, which weakened immune systems and increased vulnerability to disease. The Black Death’s rapid spread and high mortality rate have led to alternative theories about its causative agent. While Yersinia pestis remains the most widely accepted cause, some researchers have questioned this attribution. For instance, the absence of rats in Iceland during the pandemic challenges the traditional rat-flea transmission model. Other theories propose that the Black Death may have been caused by a viral agent, such as an Ebola-like virus, or even by pulmonary anthrax caused by Bacillus anthracis. The debate over the nature of the Black Death continues, with some researchers suggesting that the medieval and modern plagues were distinct diseases. Differences in seasonality, recurrence cycles, and immunity acquisition between the two pandemics have been cited as evidence. For example, the Black Death struck during hot Mediterranean summers, a climate unsuitable for rat fleas, and immunity to the disease appears to have been acquired over time, unlike modern plague outbreaks. Despite these uncertainties, the Black Death remains a pivotal event in human history, shaping the demographic, social, and economic landscape of the medieval world.
